summary: Efione Nu Reno is an adult nutritional powder drink (ALPHATITANS VENTURES INC) registered with the Philippine FDA as a food for special dietary use (FSDU) "for people on dialysis", not as a drug, a food supplement or a food for special medical purposes. Its role is to help a dialysis patient meet energy and protein targets when food alone falls short.
variants: One registration (FR-4000011355430), registered "for people on dialysis". The FDA record gives no protein, energy or electrolyte content and no lower- or higher-protein version: read the label before prescribing.
guideline: Maintenance hemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis, metabolically stable: KDOQI 2020 recommends 1.0 to 1.2 g/kg body weight per day of protein.

CKD stages 3 to 5 or on dialysis, at risk of or with protein-energy wasting (PEW): KDOQI suggests a minimum 3-month trial of oral nutritional supplements when dietary counseling alone does not reach energy and protein needs.
A dialysis-specific formula is a tool for reaching the protein and energy target; it does not replace individualized counseling by a renal dietitian.
evidence: No published trial of Efione Nu Reno was found on PubMed (search November 17, 2026); the evidence below is for oral nutritional supplements in dialysis as a class.

Cochrane review (Mah 2020): 22 randomized trials, 1,278 adults on dialysis. Oral protein-based supplements probably raise serum albumin (mean difference 0.19 g/dL, moderate certainty), more so on hemodialysis and in malnourished patients. Deaths were not reported as an outcome in any trial, so the effect on survival and other clinical outcomes is uncertain.

Meta-analysis (Liu 2023): 22 randomized trials, 1,185 patients on dialysis. Supplements raised serum albumin (1.26 g/L), body mass index and handgrip strength, with no significant change in serum phosphorus, potassium or C-reactive protein.
cautions: Potassium, phosphorus and sodium: the FDA record does not give the composition. Check the product label and count every serving in the day's potassium, phosphorus and sodium; monitor serum levels after starting.
Fluid: the water used to mix the powder counts toward the fluid allowance (for dialysis patients, the interdialytic allowance).
Stage mismatch: a product made for dialysis is not designed for a low-protein diet before dialysis; check its protein per serving before giving it to a patient with CKD not on dialysis.
Diabetes: nutritional powder drinks usually contain carbohydrate. Check glucose after starting, especially with insulin or sulfonylureas.

Cost: these are paid out of pocket in most settings. Reserve them for patients with, or at risk of, protein-energy wasting, set a goal (intake, weight, albumin, subjective global assessment), and reassess after about 3 months.
A food for special dietary use is a food, not a medicine. It supplements meals and does not replace them or individualized counseling by a renal dietitian.
bottom_line: A possible option for a dialysis patient with, or at risk of, protein-energy wasting whose intake falls short after dietitian counseling. There are no product-specific trials and the FDA record gives no composition: check the label for protein, potassium, phosphorus, sodium and fluid, set a goal, and reassess after about 3 months.
